title: Every kind of family
hookLine: every family is welcome in the sangat
tomorrow: Bhua Kiran keeps getting asked when she'll marry. where does she fit?

lines: EVERY KIND OF FAMILY IN ONE ROW.
cards: Sunday, and Simran is carrying a bucket of dal down the pangat, the long row where everyone sits on the floor to eat. Maya follows with the rotis, still learning the rhythm: kneel, offer, two hands.

Down the row: a dad on his own with twin toddlers, one in his lap, one escaping under the mat. A grandmother feeding the grandson she's raising. A mom, her new husband, and kids from both their first marriages.
A man who came alone by bus, still in his work vest. Maya leans in and whispers: is every family actually welcome here? Like, any kind?
Simran doesn't answer yet. She's watching the twins' dad try to eat with one hand.

teach.b: The answer starts with the floor. Tradition traces langar to Guru Nanak: a free kitchen where anyone eats, and everyone sits at the same level, in the same row.

teach.h: NO FAMILY CHECKED AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: Nobody's family is checked at the door. Nobody asks who is married to whom, or whose kid is whose.

teach.h: ANG 611: ONE FATHER, ALL HIS CHILDREN.
teach.b: Guru Arjan gives the reason on ang 611, in paraphrase: there is one Father, and we are all children of the One. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight.
That line doesn't say we're one family because our families look alike. It says we're one family because of who made us.
The single dad, the grandmother, the man in the work vest and Simran are in the same row for the same reason.
On ang 97, Guru Arjan says it another way, in paraphrase: everyone is called a partner and a sharer, and no one is outside You.
So the sangat isn't a club for households that look a certain way, and langar isn't a reward for getting your family right. It's a room that was already set for every kind.
Simran sets the bucket down, kneels by the twins' dad, and takes one toddler on her knee so he can eat with both hands. Maya gets it without a word, and goes back for more rotis.

how: At a gurdwara's langar anyone may eat, and people traditionally sit together on the floor in rows (pangat), served the same food whoever they are.

games.q: what does “every kind of family” mean?
o: only married couples with children can join a sangat
families sit apart at langar, by village or caste
every household belongs in the same row at langar

games.q: one row, every family — tap the pairs.
p: the row where everyone sits to eat
one Father, we are all His children
all are sharers, no one is outside
Simran held one so he could eat

s: langar is a meal mainly for Sikh families
langar is free for anyone, and everyone sits in the same row; nobody's family is checked at the door.
Guru Arjan writes that there is one Father and we are all His children
ang 611: we're one family because of who made us, not because our families look alike.
at langar, honored guests are served first, at a separate table
the point of the pangat is the same floor and the same row for everyone.

games.q: you're serving at langar. a dad on his own is juggling two toddlers and hasn't eaten. the line behind you is long. what fits today's idea?
o: kneel and hold one child so he can eat; the row is his too.
keep serving the line quickly; that's the seva you signed up for.
find someone to take him and the kids to a quieter side room.
games.why: the row was set for every kind of family. Simran took a toddler on her knee, and Maya went back for more rotis.

practice: Bring to mind one family near you that doesn't look like yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a kid's classmate.
Think of one small, ordinary welcome you could offer them, a seat saved, a plate passed, a name remembered, and hold that picture as the sit begins.

wordCard.voice: Every kind of family. The sangat's row, set for all of them, because all are children of the One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pangat, the row where everyone sits together to eat langar.

carryVoice: Every family: one Father, one row, and room on the floor for every kind. See you tomorrow.
